Edit this photograph, picture 1. Change only the back of the head and the ribbons of jelly at the neck, what the glass cylinder on the bench holds, what is seen through the round port, and the small plate on the microscope. Everything else stays exactly as it is, in the same place and at the same size: Trace, the face, the hands, the clothes, the place and every light that falls on them.

THE BACK OF THE HEAD. Trace has one head, and its outline is a seabird's. Where the clear dome swells out behind the head now, the back of the head is drawn in close: a low rounded crown and a nape that runs straight down into the back of the neck, no wider and no higher than a booby's own head. Along that outline the head changes what it is made of. Behind the eye the brown feathers go clear one by one: a few whole feathers of clear lilac jelly lying flat among the brown ones, then more, and at the back of the head they have run together into smooth, thick, milky lilac jelly, lying as close to the head as the feathers did, with the last brown feathers lying deep inside it. At the nape the jelly thins and becomes the skin of the neck. Out of that skin, in one row down the back of the neck from the nape to the collar, grow five ruffled ribbons of the same jelly, each rooted in the neck and lying flat against it. Four end at the shoulder; the longest comes forward over the collar to the fingers of the hand at the collarbone, which holds its end as before. The jelly is lit only from outside: the port's cold light shows through it from behind, and the lamp puts one warm highlight on it. The face, the eye, the bill, the white throat and both hands stay exactly as they are.

THE CYLINDER. The glass cylinder and its round stand stay exactly where they are. All that the cylinder held is gone, and every ring and mote of light that hung round it, and the glass is filled again from nothing with what the reference pictures show: a hologram with real depth, a small solid-looking scene with a near side and a far side, all of it inside the glass. Inside it is a coral growing through black space sown with fine white dust: many hundreds of bricks of light, flat-sided rectangular blocks with deep clear faces and thin bright edges, set edge to edge in rings round open holes, ring joined to ring into curving walls and tunnels full of round windows, jade teal at its heart and deep indigo and violet at its growing edges, with a spray of white needles, thin as hairs, in every hole. A pale lilac crystal shaped like a twelve-sided die glows where it is held in the coral's wall. One tiny bright craft flies through a tunnel of it and lays behind it a ribbon of small bricks set end to end. A swarm of tiny violet shards flows past in the shape of a ring, long rows of small cyan dashes run through the dark, and far behind curves the wall of a vast hollow sphere, a net of thin dim blue lines in six-sided panes.

THE PORT. Through the round port is that same growth at its true size, with exactly the look of the reference pictures: black space sown with fine white dust, and close outside a wall of bricks of light, flat-sided rectangular blocks with deep clear faces and thin bright edges, each as big as a door, set edge to edge in rings round open holes, jade teal deepening to indigo and violet, with a spray of white needles in every hole. The port's riveted frame, the jar, the hand that holds it and the bill stay where they are.

THE MICROSCOPE. The small plate on the microscope's head is plain white enamel like the rest of it, and blank.

Whatever of that sea this picture holds, beyond a window or small in a display, has exactly that look: the same shapes, the same colours, the same glow. Take the look and never the framing.
